title: Spirit as soul, and the vanity of pleasure's end
english: He calls the soul 'spirit,' because a deliberate choice is a certain movement of the mind. David says, 'Into your hands I entrust my spirit' (Psalm 30:6 LXX). And: 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit' (Acts 7:59). And in the Books of Kingdoms (1-4 Kingdoms in the LXX, corresponding to 1-2 Samuel and 1-2 Kings) it says that David did not grieve the spirit of his son Amnon (2 Kingdoms 13:39 LXX; 2 Samuel 13:39).

All such things have one end: vanity. Which is not found to abound for what comes next. Once the activity has ceased, the enjoyment is erased as well, and nothing is stored up for the future. No trace or remnant of gladness is left behind for those who took pleasure, once the activity according to pleasure has passed.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Eustathius opens his commentary on Ecclesiastes by explaining that the biblical term 'spirit' means the soul, then argues that all such human activities end in vanity.
